name: Benford's Law Analysis
description: Evaluates the distribution of the most significant digits of Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients against Benford's Law. Natural images typically conform to this logarithmic probability distribution, whereas AI-generated images or manipulated regions often exhibit statistically significant deviations.
mechanism: Extracts AC coefficients from 8x8 DCT blocks across the image and computes a histogram of their first significant digits (1-9). The empirical distribution is then compared against the theoretical Benford's Law distribution (P(d) = log10(1 + 1/d)) using the Chi-Square (χ²) goodness-of-fit test or Kullback-Leibler divergence. AI synthesis and rendering processes often inherently disrupt this natural statistical regularity.
parameters: Transform: 8x8 DCT, Target Block: AC coefficients, Statistical Distance: Chi-Square (χ²) / Kullback-Leibler Divergence
accuracy: Moderate (70-80%) - Most effective when combined with other frequency-domain forensics.
source: Perez-Gonzalez et al. (2007) Generalized Benford's Law for JPEG Coefficients
useCase: Statistical validation of image origin, detection of double JPEG compression, and synthetic generation trace identification.

references.title: Fu, D. et al. (2007). Generalized Benford's Law for JPEG Coefficients. IEEE TIFS.
Perez-Gonzalez, F. et al. (2007). Benford's Law in Image Forensics. IEEE ICIP.

strengths:
• Anchored in a naturally occurring, robust statistical phenomenon.
• Computationally efficient operations primarily in the DCT domain.
• Highly sensitive to repetitive operations like re-compression or block-level splicing.
• Functions independently of the semantic or conceptual content of the image.
limitations:
• Susceptible to false positives in images with extreme textures, absolute flatness, or heavy noise.
• Aggressive quantization and high JPEG compression ratios can overwrite or obscure synthetic deviations.
• Lower standalone accuracy for state-of-the-art GANs and advanced Diffusion models.
• Requires sufficiently large image dimensions to achieve statistical confidence.
